heading: Cold open
narration: A whale can die once and feed a deep-sea community for decades.

heading: Cold open
narration: First the flesh goes. Then the enriched sediment. Finally, microbes unlock energy trapped inside the bones.

heading: Title card
narration: What happens when a whale dies in the deep ocean?

heading: A single body changes a food-poor landscape
narration: Most organic matter produced near the surface is eaten, recycled, or broken down before it reaches the deep seafloor.

args.title: TENS OF TONS TO ONE SMALL AREA

heading: A single body changes a food-poor landscape
narration: A whale carcass is different. If it sinks intact, it can deliver tens of tons of tissue, blubber, and bone to one small area.

heading: A single body changes a food-poor landscape
narration: Researchers call the resulting ecosystem a whale fall. The phrase can sound like one event, but the biology unfolds as a succession.

args.title: TENS OF TONS TO ONE SMALL AREA

heading: A single body changes a food-poor landscape
narration: Different organisms arrive when different resources become available. Depth, temperature, carcass size, burial, and local currents change the timeline.

heading: A single body changes a food-poor landscape
narration: Some whale falls are discovered naturally. Others have been placed experimentally so scientists can return with submersibles and track change.

args.title: TENS OF TONS TO ONE SMALL AREA

heading: A single body changes a food-poor landscape
narration: The concentrated food creates an island in an otherwise sparse landscape, but it also creates chemistry that lasts after the visible flesh is gone.

heading: A single body changes a food-poor landscape
narration: The first open loop is timing: the dramatic scavengers arrive early, yet the longest part of the ecosystem begins after most viewers would think the meal is finished.

heading: Producer POV
narration: I expected the dramatic part to be the sharks and hagfish. The part I did not expect was the bone stage—an energy reserve that can keep supporting life long after the carcass stops looking like food.

args.text: I expected the dramatic part to be the sharks and hagfish. The part I did not expect was the bone stage—an energy reserve that can keep supporting life long after the carcass stops looking like food.

heading: The first stage is large and fast
narration: Sharks, hagfish, ratfish, amphipods, and other mobile scavengers detect the carcass and remove soft tissue.

args.conclusion: The area around the whale becomes enriched with organic matter

heading: The first stage is large and fast
narration: Video from whale falls often shows hagfish entering openings and twisting through tissue while larger fish tear from the outside.

heading: The first stage is large and fast

heading: The first stage is large and fast
narration: The animals do not consume every resource equally. Thick blubber, small scraps, and material pressed into sediment remain after the major muscles are gone. The area around the whale becomes enriched with organic matter.

heading: The first stage is large and fast
narration: That supports dense worms, crustaceans, and mollusks in a second phase often called enrichment opportunist.

narration: The names are categories imposed by researchers; real communities overlap. One stage does not switch off on a specific date.

heading: The first stage is large and fast
narration: The next unresolved question is why a skeleton with little visible flesh can continue feeding life for much longer than the scavenger phase.

heading: Bones store an energy reserve
narration: Whale bones contain lipids. In low-oxygen microenvironments, microbes break down that material and generate sulfide.

heading: Bones store an energy reserve
narration: Sulfide-oxidizing bacteria use chemical energy, creating a foundation for mussels, worms, snails, and other animals.

heading: Bones store an energy reserve
narration: This sulfophilic stage can persist for decades in a large carcass. Bone-eating worms in the genus Osedax penetrate bone and rely on symbiotic bacteria to help access nutrients.

heading: Bones store an energy reserve
narration: Their red plumes extend into the water while root-like tissues enter the skeleton.

heading: Bones store an energy reserve
narration: The community begins to resemble other chemosynthetic habitats, including seeps and vents, even though the original energy arrived from a surface-feeding mammal.

heading: Bones store an energy reserve
narration: Whale falls may also act as stepping stones for species that use scattered sulfide-rich habitats across the seafloor.

heading: Bones store an energy reserve
narration: That idea is plausible and studied, but not every species travels from one whale fall to another. The open loop is what remains after the chemical energy declines.

heading: From food island to hard substrate
narration: As bone lipids are exhausted and sulfide production falls, the remaining skeleton can still provide hard surface in an environment dominated by soft sediment.

heading: From food island to hard substrate
narration: Suspension feeders and other attached organisms may use the bones. Eventually the structure breaks down or becomes buried.

heading: From food island to hard substrate
narration: The full sequence shows why a whale fall cannot be summarized as sharks eating a carcass.

heading: From food island to hard substrate
narration: It links surface photosynthesis, animal migration, deep scavenging, microbial metabolism, chemosynthesis, and habitat structure.

heading: From food island to hard substrate
narration: Smithsonian descriptions use distinct stages to make that succession understandable, while emphasizing that durations vary.

heading: From food island to hard substrate
narration: A responsibly sourced video should not claim every whale fall lasts the same number of years or hosts the same species.

narration: The next episode follows a crab that does something even more deliberate with chemosynthesis—it cultivates bacteria on its own arms.

heading: One body, three ecological chapters
narration: The first chapter belongs to mobile scavengers that remove soft tissue. Smithsonian says this phase can last up to about two years.

args.title: THREE ECOLOGICAL CHAPTERS
steps: remove soft tissue, up to about two years
worms, crustaceans and mollusks use leftovers and nutrient-rich sediment
bacteria break down lipids in bones, lasting decades
args.note: The carcass shifts from meal to habitat

heading: One body, three ecological chapters
narration: The enrichment-opportunist phase follows as worms, crustaceans, and mollusks use leftovers and nutrient-rich sediment, also on the order of years.

heading: One body, three ecological chapters
narration: The sulfophilic stage can last decades. Bacteria break down lipids in bones and generate reduced chemicals that support additional microbes and animals. The carcass shifts from meal to habitat.

heading: Why the phases overlap
narration: The familiar three-stage whale-fall diagram is a model, not a stopwatch.

heading: Why the phases overlap
narration: Mobile scavengers can arrive while soft tissue remains. Smaller organisms use enriched sediment before every large piece is gone. Microbial processes inside bone begin while other feeding continues.

heading: Why the phases overlap
narration: Current, oxygen, sediment, carcass size, and local species change the pace. A small carcass in one setting will not reproduce the timeline of a large whale in another.

heading: Why the phases overlap
narration: The overlap matters because it turns the whale into more than a pile of calories.

heading: Why the phases overlap
narration: It changes local chemistry, creates hard structure on soft sediment, and can provide habitat over long periods.

heading: Why the phases overlap
narration: The edit should keep one timeline on screen while multiple processes appear together.

heading: Why the phases overlap
narration: That avoids the false impression that the ecosystem waits for a clean handoff between chapters.

heading: Why the phases overlap
narration: The final image should be the same skeleton at a later time, still functioning as habitat after the dramatic scavenger footage has ended.

heading: The continuity shot
narration: Use the same section of skeleton in each phase so the audience can see the habitat changing around it.

heading: The continuity shot
narration: Do not cut from one unrelated whale fall to another and imply a single time-lapse.

heading: The continuity shot
narration: If external footage is admitted, the caption must identify when different sites or expeditions are being compared. The original diagram remains the safest continuity device.

heading: What the camera may miss
narration: Much of the later whale-fall community is small, slow, microbial, or inside sediment and bone.

heading: What the camera may miss
narration: A dramatic ROV pass can overrepresent large scavengers and underrepresent the processes that last longest.

args.term: WHAT A DRAMATIC ROV PASS SHOWS
excludes: The small, slow, microbial processes inside sediment and bone

heading: What the camera may miss
narration: Original diagrams and sourced microscopy stills may explain the later stages better than a montage of sharks.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Use a time-lapse structure with the same whale silhouette changing across years.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Keep the phases on screen and avoid pretending that every whale fall follows the same exact clock.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Original diagrams can show the succession without using copyrighted documentary footage. If real whale-fall footage is added, its license must be admitted clip by clip.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Stage names and time ranges are simplified models.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Duration depends on whale size, depth, temperature, oxygen, burial, scavenger access, and local community.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: The phases can overlap rather than switching cleanly. A whale fall supports a rich ecosystem, but it is not accurate to claim that every carcass produces the same species sequence or lasts the same number of years.

heading: Closing
narration: A whale fall is not one feeding event. It is ecological succession written across flesh, sediment, and bone.

heading: Closing
narration: By the time the skeleton becomes the main energy source, the animal has been gone for years and the ecosystem it created is still working.
